beats.beat: Mr Rowe and the sexton find the main beam of the schoolroom cracked through with spring damp, and the repair will cost fifteen pounds against four in the poor box.
Rowe goes to the library above the draper's to post a subscription notice, where Miss Judith Vane is minding the counter for her brother.

Judith offers to keep the subscription book herself and suggests he ask certain parishioners by name rather than post a general notice; Rowe, harried, calls it parish politics dressed as advice, and she withdraws the offer at once.
Mrs Pike arrives with the news that Miss Louisa Marchmont, niece to the family holding the living, is to stay a fortnight at the gatehouse of the empty Amberlight House.
beats.note: Mrs Pike says 'the niece' and 'the family's business' but never states the family holds the living; a first-time listener has no way to know why this matters.

beats.beat: Mrs Pike declares this is the answer to everything and begins listing what Rowe must wear to be presented to her, ignoring his protest that he wants subscriptions, not a wife.

turn.note: Mrs Pike's closing line commits Rowe to both a courtship campaign and a subscription drive he never asked for, setting up the next chapter's matchmaking.

listenability: The poor box held four pounds and eleven shillings, of which two were promised to the Ludd family at the mill cottages, whose youngest had been ill since Easter. -- three levels of relative clause stacked on one sentence; split into 'The poor box held four pounds and eleven shillings. Two were already promised to the Ludd family at the mill cottages, whose youngest had been ill since Easter.'

generic_prose.quote: with the satisfaction of a woman who has found the lid that fits the pot
generic_prose.replace_with: a specific image tied to Mrs Pike's actual habits -- e.g. the satisfaction of a woman closing a ledger that has finally balanced

generic_prose.quote: which she always did, and which he had never learned to like
generic_prose.replace_with: leave the trait but anchor the dislike to something concrete he could name, since chapter 2 will supply the real cause and this line should not pre-empt it with vague irritation

trope_note: Delivers the meddling matchmaker straight through Mrs Pike's scheme and plants enemies-of-manner friction in the Rowe/Vane exchange; the chaperone's absence is lightly seeded via Louisa's solitary maid. No fourth trope introduced.
fixes: Add a clause to Mrs Pike's speech naming that Louisa's family holds the Amberlight living, so the stakes of her visit are legible without the series bible.

Combine 'had likely been getting in since before the old rector died' and 'He mentioned twice that he had spoken of it to the rector' into a single sentence -- both make the same point and the chapter is running long.
Split the poor-box sentence (quoted in listenability) into two so the ear doesn't lose the antecedent of 'whose.'
Replace the 'lid that fits the pot' simile with an image specific to Mrs Pike rather than a stock domestic metaphor.
Trim Mrs Pike's wardrobe instructions to one or two items (coat, neckcloth) rather than three, to recover some of the chapter's length overage.
Tighten Judith's Hollis/Yardley speech slightly -- keep both names, since the beat requires them, but shorten the modifying clauses attached to each.

findings.quote: Miss Judith Vane was at the counter, and she looked up at him directly, which she always did, and which he had never learned to like.
findings.note: 3 clauses coordinated in 26 words. Heard once, the last one lands with the subject of the first already gone. Split after the first clause, or make every member the same grammatical shape so the ear can follow the pattern.

writer_note:
This story is now read by a single narrator rather than a
cast with a voice each, so the prose has to carry who is speaking. It was
written under the old rule, which forbade attribution because the voices made it
redundant.

Go through the chapter and add attribution wherever a listener — who cannot see
the page, and cannot look back — would lose track of who is speaking. A tag
belongs in its own narrator segment: `said Mrs Pike`, `Rowe said`, or an action
that does the same work: *Rowe turned the note over.* Two people alternating in
a plain exchange do not need one every line; the third turn usually does, and so
does every return to dialogue after narration, and every line in a scene of
three or more.

Do not attribute every line. An unbroken column of `said X` is padding, and it
is the opposite failure.

Where a line would be misread without it, you may add a `tag` to that segment —
`"[quietly]"`, `"[a beat]"`, `"[warmly]"` — as performance direction for the
voice. It is never printed and never spoken. A few a chapter at most, and never
to imitate a different person: one voice reads everyone.

Come back no longer than you started. These chapters are already at or over
their word ceiling, and attribution adds words — so take them back out of
restatement: a line of dialogue that lands followed by narration explaining that
it landed, a room established twice. If you come back long the check sends the
chapter straight back to be cut, which spends a revision on arithmetic instead
of on the prose.

Change nothing else. Same events, same beats, same jokes, same last line.
